success_patterns: Slot type was named correctly before answering: 'she' -> the actress, 'this famed horticulturist' -> the person, 'this 1997 movie' -> the film title, 'this capital city' -> the city only. Related entities such as the song, the plum or the family were treated as anchors.

Where several candidates fit (two Peter Fonda 1997 films, various Nobel family members), the agent chose the one matching every clue detail (Oscar nomination, born 1940, Wessex Poems 1898), and the entity recurring across many passages won.
A quoted pun word in the clue ('steak') and a title clue ('Marquess of this') were resolved to the territorial name (Salisbury), not the family or personal surname.
Double-meaning clue handled by finding one word that fits both halves ('test'), and noisy passages were backed by own knowledge.
Answers were bare and short: no quotation marks, no honorific or post-nominal (Thomas Hardy, not 'Thomas Hardy, OM'), no added type word ('vanilla', not 'vanilla ice cream').

patch.reasoning: The skill already covers nearly every behavior seen in this batch, and earlier long additions were rejected. The one reusable pattern not stated explicitly is peerage-title clues ('The Marquess/Duke/Earl of this'). Their slot is the territorial name, but passages are full of the holder's surname and personal name, which invites a wrong answer. A short insertion in Rule 2 covers it without adding length elsewhere.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Peerage or office-of-place clues ('The Marquess of this...', 'the Duke of this', 'the Earl of this', 'the Bishop of this') ask for the PLACE or territorial name the title is tied to (the Marquess of Salisbury -> 'Salisbury'), not the holder's family surname, personal name or the rank word. Pick the place the passages pair with the clue's other facts (first PM of the century, etc.). A quoted pun word in the clue (a 'steak') often confirms it (Salisbury steak).
